## Adaptive Control of Robot Manipulators With Uncertain Kinematics and Dynamics

## Abstract

In this paper, we investigate the adaptive control problem for robot manipulators with both the uncertain kinematics and dynamics. We propose two adaptive control schemes to realize the objective of task-space trajectory tracking irrespective of the uncertain kinematics and dynamics. The proposed controllers have the desirable separation property, and we also show that the first adaptive controller with appropriate modifications can yield improved performance, without the expense of conservative gain choice. The performance of the proposed controllers is shown by numerical simulations.

## 1 Index Terms

Adaptive control, separation approach, kinematic uncertainty, robot manipulators, performance.

## I. INTRODUCTION

The study on the adaptive control of robot manipulators with dynamic parameter uncertainty has a long and rich history (see, e.g., the early results in [1], [2], [3]), and the employment of adaptive control provides robot manipulators with the ability of performing tasks in the unknown environment. The recent advances in adaptive robot control occur in [4], [5], [6], [7], [8] aiming at handling the kinematic parameter uncertainty. Kinematic uncertainty is frequently encountered as the robots perform various work in the task space (e.g., Cartesian space or image space) (see, e.g., [4], [9]), among which is the now actively studied visual servoing problem (see, e.g., [9], [10], [11]). These control schemes (e.g., [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [10], [11]) are characterized by the use of an approximate Jacobian matrix (due to the kinematics uncertainty), and the prominent Authors' Capabilities

Differentiating (1) with respect to time gives the relation between the task-space velocity and joint-space velocity [12], [15]

\[ \dot{x} = J(q)\dot{q} \tag{2} \]

where \( J(q) \in R^{n \times n} \) is the Jacobian matrix. In the case that the kinematic parameters are unknown, we cannot obtain the task-space position/velocity by the direct kinematics given above. Instead, we assume that certain task-space sensors (e.g., a camera) are employed to give the task-space position/velocity information. The kinematics (2) has the following linearity-in-parameters property [5].

**Property 1:** The kinematics (2) depends linearly on a constant parameter vector \( a_k \), which gives rise to

\[ J(q)\xi = Y_k(q,\xi)a_k \tag{3} \]

where \( \xi \in R^n \) is a vector and \( Y_k(q,\xi) \) is the kinematic regressor matrix.

The equations of motion of the manipulator can be written as [16], [15]

\[ M(q)\ddot{q} + C(q,\dot{q})\dot{q} + g(q) = \tau \tag{4} \]

where \( M(q) \in R^{n \times n} \) is the inertia matrix, \( C(q,\dot{q}) \in R^{n \times n} \) is the Coriolis and centrifugal matrix, \( g(q) \in R^n \) is the gravitational torque, and \( \tau \in R^n \) is the joint control torque. For the convenience of later reference, three well-understood properties associated with the dynamics (4) are listed as follows (see, e.g., [16], [15]).

**Property 2:** The inertia matrix \( M(q) \) is symmetric and uniformly positive definite.

where \( \xi \in R^n \) is a vector and \( Y_k(q,\xi) \) is the kinematic regressor matrix.

The equations of motion of the manipulator can be written as [16], [15]

\[ M(q)\ddot{q} + C(q,\dot{q})\dot{q} + g(q) = \tau \tag{4} \]

For the convenience of later reference, three well-understood properties associated with the dynamics (4) are listed as follows (see, e.g., [16], [15]).

**Property 2:** The inertia matrix \( M(q) \) is symmetric and uniformly positive definite.

**Property 3:** The Coriolis and centrifugal matrix \( C(q,\dot{q}) \) can be appropriately determined such that \( \dot{M}(q) - 2C(q,\dot{q}) \) is skew-symmetric.

**Property 4:** The dynamics (4) depends linearly on a constant parameter vector \( a_d \), which leads to

\[ M(q)\dot{\xi} + C(q,\dot{q})\xi + g(q) = Y_d(q,\dot{q},\dot{\xi}, \dot{\zeta})a_d \tag{5} \]

where \( \zeta \in R^n \) is a differentiable vector, \( \dot{\xi} \) is the time derivative of \( \zeta \), and \( Y_d(q,\dot{q},\dot{\xi},\dot{\zeta}) \) is the dynamic regressor matrix.

Adaptive Controller \(I\)Following [5], [6], we define a joint reference velocity using the estimated Jacobian matrix as \[\dot{q}_{r}=\hat{J}^{-1}(q)\dot{x}_{r} \quad (6)\] where \(\dot{x}_{r}=\dot{x}_{d}-\alpha\Delta x\), \(\Delta x=x-x_{d}\) denotes the task-space position tracking error, \(\alpha\) is a positive design constant, and \(\hat{J}(q)\) is the estimated Jacobian matrix which is obtained by replacing \(a_{k}\) in \(J(q)\) with its estimate \(\hat{a}_{k}\). Differentiating equation (6) with respect to time gives the joint reference acceleration \[\ddot{q}_{r}=\hat{J}^{-1}(q)\Big{[}\ddot{x}_{r}-\dot{\hat{J}}(q)\dot{q}_{r}\Big {]}.\] (7) Let us now define a sliding vector \[s =\dot{q}-\dot{q}_{r}\] (8) and using (2), (3), and (6), we can rewrite equation (8) as \[s =J^{-1}(q)\left[\dot{x}-J(q)\dot{q}_{r}\right]=J^{-1}(q)\left[\dot{x}- \hat{J}(q)\dot{q}_{r}+Y_{k}(q,\dot{q}_{r})\Delta a_{k}\right]\] \[=J^{-1}(q)\left[\Delta\dot{x}+\alpha\Delta x+Y_{k}(q,\dot{q}_{r}) \Delta a_{k}\right]\] (9) which can further be written as [20], [21] \[\Delta\dot{x} =-\alpha\Delta x-Y_{k}(q,\dot{q}_{r})\Delta a_{k}+J(q)s\] \[\Delta a_{k} =\hat{a}_{k}-a_{k}\text{ is the kinematic parameter estimation error.}\] The control law is given as \[\tau =-Ks+Y_{d}(q,\dot{q},\dot{q}_{r},\ddot{q}_{r})\hat{a }_{d}\] (10) where \(K\in R^{n\times n}\) is a symmetric positive definite matrix. The estimated dynamic parameter \(\hat{a}_{d}\) (i.e., the estimate of \(a_{d}\)) is updated by \[\hat{a}_{d} =-\Gamma_{d}Y_{d}^{T}(q,\dot{q},\dot{q}_{r},\ddot{q}_{r})s \quad (12)\]

### Page 6

where $Γ_d$ is a symmetric positive definite matrix. The estimated kinematic parameter $\hat{a}_k$ is updated by the direct adaptation law
\[\dot{a}_k = Γ_k Y_k^T (q, \dot{q}_r)[(\beta/\alpha)\Delta\dot{x} + \Delta x]\]

where $Γ_k$ is a symmetric positive definite matrix and $\beta \in [0, 1]$ is a design constant.

**Remark 1:** The differences between the adaptive controller here and the one in [5], [6] are that 1) the feedback part in (11) can be rewritten as $-KJ^{-1}(q)[\Delta\dot{x} + \alpha\Delta x + Y_k(q, \dot{q}_r)\Delta a_k]$, which can thus be intuitively interpreted as inverse Jacobian feedback of both the task-space tracking error and the kinematic parameter estimation error rather than the approximate transpose Jacobian feedback and 2) the kinematic parameter adaptation law (13) is based on an adaptive regressor that depends on the joint reference velocity $\dot{q}_r$ rather than $\dot{q}$. The dynamic parameter adaptation law (12) is actually the same as the one in [6]. The control law (11) expands the inverse Jacobian based task-space adaptive scheme in [2, Sec. 3] to additionally include the inverse Jacobian feedback of the kinematic parameter estimation error, which supplies our controller with the ability of handling the kinematic uncertainties.

Substituting the control law (11) into the dynamics (4) yields
\[M(q)\dot{s} + C(q, \dot{q})s = -Ks + Y_d(q, \dot{q}, \dot{q}_r, \ddot{q}_r)\Delta a_d\]

where $\Delta a_d = \hat{a}_d - a_d$. The closed-loop robotic system can be described by
\[\left\{
\begin{aligned}
\Delta\dot{x} &= -\alpha\Delta x - Y_k(q, \dot{q}_r)\Delta a_k + J(q)s, \\
M(q)\dot{s} + C(q, \dot{q})s &= -Ks + Y_d(q, \dot{q}, \dot{q}_r, \ddot{q}_r)\Delta a_d, \\
\end{aligned}
\right.\]

and the adaptation laws (12) and (13).

We are presently ready to formulate the following theorem.

**Theorem 1:** Suppose that the estimated Jacobian matrix $\hat{J}(q)$ is nonsingular and that all joints of the manipulator are revolute. Then, the control law (11), the dynamic parameter adaptation law (12), and the kinematic parameter adaptation law (13) ensure that the task-space tracking errors converge to zero, i.e., $\Delta x \to 0$ and $\Delta \dot{x} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty$.

**Proof:** Following [2], [22], we take into account the Lyapunov-like function candidate $V_1 = (1/2)s^T M(q)s + (1/2)\Delta a_d^T\Gamma_d^{-1}\Delta a_d$, and differentiating $V_1$ with respect to time along the trajectories of the second subsystem in (15) and of the adaptation law (12) and using Property 3, we obtain $\dot{V}_1 = -s^T Ks \leq 0$, which implies that $s \in L_2 \cap L_\infty$ and $\hat{a}_d \in L_\infty$.

## Appendix B Adaptive Controller II

We now present an adaptive controller that also has the separation property but uses different joint reference velocity and kinematic parameter adaptation law. This controller relies on the joint reference velocity defined as

\[\dot{q}_{r} = \hat{J}^{-1}(q)\dot{x}_{d} - \alpha \hat{J}^{T}(q)\Delta x. \]

We then have that

\[\Delta \dot{x} = -\alpha \hat{J}(q)\hat{J}^{T}(q)\Delta x - Y_{k}(q,\dot{q})\Delta a_{k} + \hat{J}(q)s.\hspace{10mm} (20)\]

The control law and the dynamic parameter adaptation law are still (11) and (12) yet with \(\dot{q}_{r}\) given by (20). The kinematic parameter adaptation law is given as

\[\dot{a}_{k} = \Gamma_{k}Y_{k}^{T}(q,\dot{q})\Delta x. \hspace{10mm} (21)\]

**Theorem 2:** The control law (11) and dynamic parameter adaptation law (12) with \(\dot{q}_{r}\) given by (20), and kinematic parameter adaptation law (22) ensure that \(\Delta x \to 0\) and \(\Delta \dot{x} \to 0\) as \(t \to \infty\) provided that the estimated Jacobian matrix \(\hat{J}(q)\) is nonsingular. **Proof:** For the dynamic loop, we can directly obtain that \(s \in \mathcal{L}_{2} \cap \mathcal{L}_{\infty}\) and \(\hat{a}_{d} \in \mathcal{L}_{\infty}\), by following similar procedures as in the proof of Theorem 1. Then, there exists a positive constant \(l_{M}^{*}\) such that \(\int_{0}^{t}s^{T}(r)s(r)dr \leq l_{M}^{*}, \forall t \geq 0\). Consider the following quasi-Lyapunov function candidate

\[V_{2}^{*} = \frac{1}{2}\Delta x^{T}\Delta x + \frac{1}{2\alpha} \left[ l_{M}^{*} - \int_{0}^{t}s^{T}(r)s(r)dr \right] + \frac{1}{2}\Delta a_{k}^{T}\Gamma_{k}^{-1}\Delta a_{k} \hspace{10mm} (23)\]

and we obtain

M(q) = J^T(q)M(q)J^T(q)

The molecular dynamic simulation was run for 120 ps using coarse-grained GROMACS 2019-2-1 with the Amber-Dynamics molecular dynamics (MD) software package. The system consisted of 254 water molecules (with diphenylsilanol, phenylsilanol, and non-polar methane) and 26 water molecules (non-peptide molecule). The protein was initially unbound, and the system was equilibrated. The structures were heated by 200 K/ps to 330 K and slowly cooled back to 250 K/ps to complete equilibration. The sampling from 500 to 5000 Ry took place over 0.5 ps, and the energy was sampled from 300 to 3000 Ry over 0.5 ps.

The 2nd and 1st order rate constants for the real product were estimated using the simultaneous reaction-transient and hard spiking models, resulting in a value of 2.14 × 10$^{-11}$ for Scenario A. Additionally, a subsample in Scenario B was inspected and the rate constant value was found to be 3.92 × 10$^{-10}$ for 100 ps.

The KP$_{Na}$ and KL$_{Na}$ values obtained for 100 ps are then estimated using the non-switched and switched models, resulting in a value of 5.15 × 10$^{-4}$ for Scenario A and 1.13 × 10$^{-4}$ for Scenario B, respectively.

In Scenario A, bound rate constants for calmodulin with sodium, potassium, and chloride, as well as non-polar methane, are found to be 4.41 × 10$^{-11}$, 1.88 × 10$^{-11}$, and 3.47 × 10$^{-11}$, respectively. The enter domaine and loosely bound rate constants for potassium, sodium, and chloride are found to be 9.35 × 10$^{-11}$, 1.10 × 10$^{-11}$, and 6.28 × 10$^{-11}$, respectively. The central domain rate constant for toluene is found to be 1.57 × 10$^{-11}$, while the exchanger rate constant for phenylsilanol to toluene is determined to be 1.75 × 10$^{-8}$. The temperature dependence of the rate constant is not provided.

The cooperative isotherm dissociation constant results in a subcharacteristic volume of 1.59 × 10$^{-9}$ ml/g.

The PPB Lehninger Experimental Biochemistry volume parameter, which is determined by the dissociation constants of the protein powder in a non-reducing and reducing solution, is found to be 1.34.

The PPB Lehninger Non-Peptone haemoglobin volume parameter, which is determined by the dissociation of haemoglobin in the specimen, is found to be 7.35.

The PPB Lehninger Extraction Volume parameter, which is determined by the extraction of haemoglobin in the specimen, is found to be 3.88.
